title: DeepMargin — Serving fit + runbook probe
summary: Initial discovery to validate Redwood serving fit for migrating from a mixed OpenAI-hosted + on-prem vLLM/TGI stack. Primary concerns: streaming and function-calling parity, KV cache behavior, observable runbook and rollback, and security/KMS/SSO requirements.
topics: Private deployment details: VPC, KMS, audit logs
next_steps: Redwood to share security questionnaire and SOC 2 artifacts by 2026-06-05
SE to run a parity benchmark (1k prompts) using DeepMargin test set and share results by 2026-06-12
Schedule technical deep-dive on private deployment (vLLM/TGI compat) week of 2026-06-15
AE to send preliminary pricing and dedicated tier options by 2026-06-08
action_items: Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE): set up benchmark harness and run parity tests (due 2026-06-12)
Maya Chen (Redwood AE): send security pack and SOC 2 summary (due 2026-06-05)
Tom Brooks (DeepMargin CTO): provision a sample dataset and S3 access for benchmarks (due 2026-06-07)
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-02 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez, Priya Kapoor (Redwood); Sara Patel, Tom Brooks, Ajay Narayanan, Lina Gomez (DeepMargin)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. Diego is our systems SE and Priya from CSM. How are you folks doing?
[00:10] Sara: Good thanks, hey. Sorry running a tad late, we were finishing another sync.
[00:14] Tom: All good, Tom here. Excited to talk through how we might move off our current stack.
[00:20] Maya: Awesome. Quick agenda — migration constraints, parity concerns (streaming/function calls/embeddings), security/runbook for private, and next steps. Sound good?
[00:28] Lina: Yep, go for it.
[00:31] Diego: Cool. To kick off, can you walk us through what "current" looks like for DeepMargin — infra, models, and what you're running in prod?
[00:40] Sara: Sure. Right now we have a hybrid. Most user-facing stuff calls OpenAI for chat completions — it's reliable for us and handles function call stuff. But for heavy batch and lower latency internal features we run vLLM in our data center with TGI for some custom quantized models. So it's kind of two tracks.
[01:02] Ajay: Yeah infra side — we have S3, internal KMS for keys, and an ASA network, with our CI triggering deploys to vLLM nodes. We do a lot of ad-hoc caching with Redis.
[01:14] Diego: Okay that makes sense. Biggest drivers for exploring Redwood?
[01:18] Sara: Two things — unify the runtime so product teams don't have to reason about two APIs, and lower total cost while maintaining parity with the OpenAI experience. Also, we want better observability and an explicit runbook for failover.
[01:30] Maya: Great. Parity — what are your must-haves? Streaming, function calling, structured outputs, embedding similarity?
[01:36] Sara: Streaming and function-calls are non-negotiable. Our workflow depends on partial tokens coming back so the UI can show progressive suggestions. Function calling — the JSON schema approach — we rely on that. Embeddings are less urgent but used in search ranking.
[01:49] Tom: Also, we use KV cache semantics from vLLM — we keep a warm KV cache for long sessions. Curious how Redwood manages prefix caching and KV semantics.
[02:00] Diego: Right, Redwood runtime supports KV/prefix caching and continuous batching; the cache behavior is configurable. We also have automatic fallback policies if a model variant isn't available. That can be tuned per-route.
[02:12] Ajay: When you say fallback, is that seamless? Our tolerance for failed calls is low, we need graceful degradation to lighter models rather than 500s.
[02:20] Diego: Yes — the router prefers latency SLO-compatible variants first, then cost-friendly variants. We try to avoid errors by falling back, and we can instrument per-token fallback metrics in the console.
[02:32] Sara: Sounds promising. What about function-calling differences? We've seen different providers stringify or escape differently and that breaks our parsers.
[02:41] Maya: We've run evals for function calling parity; SEs can run a targeted test against your schema. Typically the differences are small — whitespace, ordering — but we include a serializer compatibility layer in the SDKs.
[02:54] Tom: Can you support our custom schema enforcement? We need the runtime to validate the output against our json-schema before returning to product.
[03:01] Diego: We have a post-processing hook that can validate — you can reject/reserialize and return a structured error. That can be part of the canary.
[03:10] Lina: On private deployment — we're most concerned about KMS integration and audit logs. Our compliance team requires HSM-backed keys for certain customers.
[03:19] Priya: We support customer-managed KMS/HSM integration; can you outline your KMS provider and whether it's reachable from a VPC?
[03:27] Ajay: We use AWS KMS with CloudHSM for some things. Keys are reachable from our VPC but there are strict egress rules.
[03:34] Diego: That's ok — Redwood Private can be deployed into a customer VPC with a private control plane model. We can integrate with your KMS endpoints and emit audit logs to your Splunk/CloudWatch. We'll need network details to propose the runbook.
[03:47] Tom: Do you support air-gapped on-prem for regulated customers?
[03:51] Maya: We have an on-prem package for very regulated customers; it includes offline deployments, but it's heavier operationally. We usually recommend VPC-first unless air-gap is a strict requirement.
[04:01] Sara: Our timeline — if we decide to move, we want pilot in Q3, full migration by end of Q4. Does that align?
[04:08] Maya: That's doable. Typical pilot is 6–8 weeks for parity tests and performance tuning.
[04:14] Diego: For the parity benchmark — what's your typical prompt distribution / token length?
[04:19] Sara: 70% short (<=64 tokens) for UI suggestions, 25% medium (64–512), and 5% long (>512) for summarization.
[04:28] Diego: Good, we'll mirror that in the harness. Do you have a test corpus we can use?
[04:33] Tom: We can provision a sampled set and S3 read-only. Ajay will help.
[04:38] Ajay: Yep I'll provision creds for a temporary bucket.
[04:41] Maya: Great — on metrics for the benchmark we'll measure latency (p50/p95), tokens/sec throughput, token-cost delta, and output-delta (BLEU/F1 or custom evals). Any other must-have metrics?
[04:53] Sara: Also function-call success rate and streaming continuity (no resets mid-stream).
[04:58] Diego: Understood. A note on vLLM/TGI compatibility — many customers that previously self-hosted vLLM ask about running their vLLM-optimized models on Redwood Dedicated or Private. We support common formats and can recommend quantization profiles. For some edge kernels, we may need to recompile or use a compatible runtime shim.
[05:18] Tom: So if our models rely on fused kernels in vLLM, will that break?
[05:22] Diego: Possibly — depends on the kernel. We can test a sample checkpoint. Sometimes we run a quick operator replacement layer or suggest a quantization profile that keeps behavior similar. That's part of the model onboarding scope.
[05:33] Lina: What's the expected variance in output when changing quantization? Our product team is sensitive to hallucination changes.
[05:39] Diego: Typical behavior can shift slightly; we run A/B evals against your golden prompts and measure regressions. We'll flag any regression over an agreed threshold.
[05:48] Sara: On cost — what's the delta for Dedicated vs Hosted? We want committed capacity because we have predictable throughput.
[05:55] Maya: Dedicated is priced as a reserved capacity contract — lower per-token costs for committed utilization plus options for burst. Hosted is pay-as-you-go. We can send an initial pricing sheet showing illustrative costs given your monthly token volumes.
[06:07] Tom: Can you do quotas and route certain high-sensitivity traffic to private and others to hosted?
[06:13] Diego: Yes — routing policies can be configured by route tags; you can set sensitive routes to Private and less-sensitive to Hosted. We also support per-token cost tracking in the console.
[06:24] Ajay: For SSO and RBAC — we use SAML2.0 with attribute-based group mapping.
[06:30] Priya: Redwood supports SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC with groups. We can map your attribute names during SSO setup.
[06:38] Sara: About reliability — your SLA? We can't have long windows of downtime during rollouts.
[06:43] Maya: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets. Hosted has strong uptime historically; we can share the SLA doc in the security pack. We also have automatic canary rollouts and immediate rollback policies.
[06:54] Tom: Ok. A few pain points we've seen: 1) function-call mismatch, 2) tokenization differences that affect billing & embeddings, 3) runbook clarity for rollbacks. Can we capture that in the pilot scope?
[07:05] Maya: Yes — pilot scope will include compatibility tests for function calling + tokenizer parity, embedding similarity tests, and a runbook/DR plan review.
[07:13] Sara: Great. Process-wise who will be our main contacts for the pilot?
[07:18] Maya: I'll be your AE lead, Diego will run the benchmarks and technical onboarding, and Priya will own the pilot ops.
[07:25] Ajay: For network/access we'll coordinate with Diego.
[07:28] Diego: I'll send a checklist for network egress rules and KMS endpoints.
[07:33] Lina: Any gotchas for long-session KV caching? We're worried about consistency when routing across instances.
[07:39] Diego: We use a centralized cache or sticky routing to keep session state — for Redwood Dedicated we can configure sticky sessions at the route level; for Private you control whether to co-locate cache resources. We'll also surface cache hit/miss ratios.
[07:52] Tom: Can we get per-token debug traces for a sample session? That would help debug when outputs diverge.
[07:58] Diego: Yes, the tracing hooks let you capture token timings, kernel selection, batching window, and cache events for a sample session. That can be turned on for pilot only.
[08:08] Maya: Quick logistics — I'll share the security doc and a pricing snapshot within a few days. Diego will start the harness once we have the S3 sample. Priya will coordinate the pilot timeline.
[08:17] Sara: Sounds good. Any miscellaneous questions from anyone?
[08:20] Ajay: One last thing — how do you handle data retention for logs and audit trails? We have retention policies for PII.
[08:27] Priya: We can configure log retention per customer and export to your storage; PII redaction is supported in audit logs and we can integrate with your DAS.
[08:35] Tom: Ok thanks. I think that's the main list.
[08:39] Maya: Recap of next steps: security pack by 6/5, pricing by 6/8, benchmark run by 6/12, technical deep-dive week of 6/15. We'll aim to align pilot kickoff with your Q3 window.
[08:51] Sara: Works for us. We'll assign owners on our side and get that S3 access to Diego.
[08:57] Maya: Great. Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links.
[09:01] Tom: Thanks everyone.
[51:30] <<meeting ended>>

Notes: transcription may have small speaker attribution errors; product names occasionally mis-heard (e.g., "Redwood Infernce" in quick speech). Shared artifacts: security pack (link: https://redwood.example/security-pack), pilot-harness README (doc: redwood-pilot-harness.md), redwood-benchmarks.xlsx (link shared in follow-up).
